title: Timber and masonry structures
summary: Masonry dominates this subchapter, and the two reliable marks are the cavity-wall effective thickness rule and the principle that mortar must be WEAKER than the masonry unit — a rule that sounds wrong until the reason is understood. For Nepal, the seismic provisions of NBC 202 matter more than anything else here: horizontal bands and vertical bars turn a collection of wall panels into a box, and that distinction is what determines whether a masonry building survives an earthquake.

sections.heading: Timber as a structural material
sections.body:
**Timber is anisotropic**, which is the fact from which everything else follows: its strength **along the grain** far exceeds that **across** it.

| Direction | Relative strength |
|---|---|
| **Compression parallel to grain** | High |
| **Compression perpendicular to grain** | Much lower — often the governing check at a bearing |
| **Tension parallel to grain** | Highest, but rarely used at capacity because connections fail first |
| Tension perpendicular to grain | Very low — to be avoided entirely |
| **Shear parallel to grain** | Low — governs at notches and connections |

The practical consequences: a **bearing** across the grain at a support may govern the design of a beam whose bending is comfortable; and a **notch** cut into a joist creates a stress concentration in the weakest direction, which is why notching is restricted.

**IS 883** classifies timber by three **grades of location**, which set the permissible stresses:

| Grade | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Inside** | Protected from weather and not exposed to damp |
| **Outside** | Exposed to weather but not continuously wet |
| **Wet** | Continuously or intermittently wet |

Permissible stresses are highest for the **inside** location and are reduced for the others, because **moisture content reduces strength**.

**Factors affecting timber strength:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Moisture content** | Strength **falls** as MC rises, up to the fibre saturation point (~30%) |
| **Defects** — knots, shakes, wane, sloping grain | Reduce strength; the basis of visual grading |
| **Duration of loading** | Timber carries a **higher** stress for a **short** duration; permissible stresses may be increased for wind or seismic |
| **Density** | Correlates strongly with strength |
| Temperature | Higher temperature reduces strength |
| **Direction of grain** | As above |

The **duration of loading** factor is peculiar to timber and worth noting: unlike steel, timber exhibits marked **creep rupture** — it will fail eventually under a load it can carry briefly. IS 883 therefore permits an increase in permissible stress for short-duration loads and requires a reduction for permanent ones.

**Seasoning** removes moisture to a level in equilibrium with the surroundings, so the timber is dimensionally stable and resistant to decay. Methods: **natural (air) seasoning** (slow, 2–4 years, reliable), **kiln seasoning** (fast and thorough, costlier), **water seasoning**, **boiling**, **chemical (salt) seasoning**, and **electrical seasoning** — the last being very quick but very costly, and its **drawback is that it causes splitting**.

**Preservation** protects against fungi, insects and marine borers. Preservatives: **creosote oil** (effective, but dark and unpaintable), **copper-chrome-arsenic (CCA)** and **ammoniacal copper** salts (clean, paintable), and **zinc chloride**. Application by **brushing, spraying, dipping, hot-and-cold open tank**, or — most effective — **pressure impregnation**, which drives the preservative deep into the sapwood rather than merely coating it.

**Engineered wood products** overcome timber's variability and size limits:

| Product | Character |
|---|---|
| **Plywood** | Odd number of veneers with **grains at right angles** — near-equal strength both ways, no splitting |
| **Blockboard / particle board** | Core of strips or chips |
| **Fibreboard** | **Hardboard > 800 kg/m³, medium 350–800, insulation board < 350** (IS 3348) |
| **Glulam** | Laminations glued into large curved or straight members |
| Laminated veneer lumber (LVL) | Veneers all in one direction; high strength |

The **cross-grain construction of plywood** is why it does not split and why it is used for formwork: an ordinary board splits along the grain, a plywood sheet cannot.

**Timber connections** are the usual weak point, since the material is weak in shear parallel to the grain and cannot develop the full member strength through a small area. Types: **nailed** (many small fasteners spread the load), **bolted** (needs washers to avoid crushing across the grain), **screwed**, **glued** (strong but needs controlled conditions), and **connectors** — split rings, shear plates, toothed plates — which spread the load over a larger bearing area than a bolt alone.

sections.heading: Masonry — materials and strength
sections.body:
Masonry is a **composite of units and mortar**, and its behaviour is not simply that of either.

**The counter-intuitive but fundamental rule:**

> **Mortar must be WEAKER than the masonry unit — not stronger.**

**Why.** Movement in a wall is inevitable — thermal, moisture, settlement, small structural strains. A **weaker mortar** accommodates it, and any cracking is **fine, distributed and confined to the joints**, where it is inconspicuous and easily repointed. A **mortar stronger than the unit** forces the cracking to occur **through the bricks or blocks**, producing fewer but wider cracks that pass through the units themselves — much harder to repair and far more damaging to appearance and weather-tightness.

A rich cement mortar is therefore not "better". IS 2250 mortar grades run from **MM 0.7 to MM 7.5** (the number being the compressive strength in N/mm²), and the grade is chosen to suit the **unit strength and the exposure**, not maximised.

**Mortar types:**

| Mortar | Character |
|---|---|
| **Cement mortar** (1:3 to 1:8) | Strong, sets in any weather; too rigid if rich |
| **Lime mortar** | **Flexible**, self-healing, breathable; slow setting; ideal for historic and low-rise work |
| **Cement-lime (gauged) mortar** | The best compromise — strength with workability and flexibility |
| Mud mortar | Traditional; very weak but locally available |

**Cement-lime mortar** deserves note because it is the traditionally preferred masonry mortar: the lime gives **workability, water retention and flexibility** while the cement provides early strength. Pure cement mortar of the same strength is harsher to work and more prone to shrinkage cracking.

**Masonry units:**

| Unit | Compressive strength |
|---|---|
| **First class brick** (IS 1077) | **≥ 10.5 N/mm²** |
| Second class | ≥ 7.0 |
| Third class | ≥ 3.5 (the code minimum class) |
| Concrete block, solid | 4 – 15 |
| Hollow concrete block | 3.5 – 5 |
| **Stone** | 20 – 100+ depending on type |

**Masonry strength is not the unit strength.** The wall's compressive strength depends on the **unit strength, the mortar grade, the slenderness ratio, the eccentricity of loading, and the shape and proportion of the unit**. IS 1905 gives the **basic compressive stress** from the unit strength and the mortar grade, then applies **stress reduction factors** for slenderness and eccentricity, plus an **area reduction factor** for small piers and a **shape modification factor**.

> **Permissible stress = basic stress × stress reduction factor × area factor × shape factor**

**Slenderness ratio:**

> **λ = effective height (or effective length) / effective thickness ≤ 27** for a load-bearing wall in cement mortar

with lower limits (up to 20) for weaker mortars and for load-bearing walls in buildings of more than a certain height.

**Effective thickness** — the most examined item in the subchapter:

| Wall | Effective thickness |
|---|---|
| **Solid wall** | The **actual** thickness |
| **Cavity wall** | **The GREATER of ⅔(t₁ + t₂) and the thickness of the thicker leaf** |
| Wall with piers | Actual thickness × a stiffening coefficient |

**The ⅔ factor formalises the fact that the two leaves of a cavity wall are TIED but NOT BONDED**, so they do not act fully together. A candidate who takes the sum of the two leaves — or only the thicker one, without comparing — will get it wrong, and both errors appear as distractors.

**Wall thicknesses** in modular brickwork (unit 190 × 90 × 90 mm, 10 mm joint):

| Wall | Actual | Nominal |
|---|---|---|
| **Half brick** | 90 mm | **100 mm** |
| **One brick** | **190 mm** | **200 mm** |
| One and a half brick | 290 mm | 300 mm |

With the **traditional** brick (about 230 × 110 × 70 mm) the thicknesses are **115 mm and 230 mm** — the "4½ inch" and "9 inch" walls of common usage. Always note which brick a question specifies.

**A half-brick wall cannot be load-bearing** over a normal storey height, because it cannot satisfy the slenderness limit. It serves only as a **partition** or as one **leaf of a cavity wall**.

sections.heading: Masonry design and construction
sections.body:
**Modes of failure in masonry**, each with its own check:

| Failure | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Compression** | Direct crushing, or buckling of a slender wall |
| **Tension / flexure** | Out-of-plane bending from wind or earthquake; masonry is very weak in tension |
| **Shear** | In-plane racking, as in an earthquake — diagonal cracking |
| **Sliding** | Along a mortar bed joint |
| **Local bearing** | Under a concentrated load from a beam or lintel |

Masonry's **tensile and shear weakness** is what makes it vulnerable in earthquakes, and it is why unreinforced masonry is assigned a **response reduction factor R of only 1.5** — it has almost no ductility.

**Design checks for a load-bearing wall:**

1. Compute the load per metre run, including self weight.
2. Determine the **slenderness ratio** and check it against the limit.
3. Determine the **eccentricity** of the load, from the bearing arrangement of the slab or beam.
4. Compute the **permissible stress** with all four modification factors.
5. Compare with the actual stress.
6. Check **concentrated loads** (bearing) and any **out-of-plane** bending.

**Eccentricity** deserves attention because it is often overlooked. A slab bearing on only part of a wall's thickness applies its load **eccentrically**, which both reduces the permissible stress and induces bending. The remedy is a **full bearing**, a **bearing plate** to spread the load, or an explicit allowance for the eccentricity.

**Openings** weaken a wall in two ways: they remove material, and they concentrate stress at the corners. IS 1905 restricts the **total area and disposition of openings**, and requires piers between openings to be checked as separate members. **Lintels** must have adequate bearing — at least the lintel depth or 100 mm.

**Construction requirements**, each with its reason:

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Bricks soaked before use** | So they do not absorb water from the mortar, leaving the cement unhydrated at the interface |
| **Joints fully filled**, 10 mm thick | Voids concentrate stress and admit water |
| **Frog laid upward** | So mortar fills it and forms a key |
| **Vertical joints staggered**, ¼ brick lap | Breaks the continuity that would make the wall a stack of piers |
| **Courses truly horizontal and level** | So the load acts normal to the bed |
| **Not more than 1–1.5 m height per day** | Green mortar cannot carry the weight above; the wall would squeeze and bulge |
| **Curing for 7–10 days** | Cement mortar needs water to gain strength |
| **Toothing or racking back** at a stopping point | So the next day's work bonds properly, rather than forming a vertical joint |

The **daily height limit** is a genuine structural requirement rather than a convenience. Freshly laid mortar has almost no strength; building too high in a day compresses the lower joints unevenly and can bulge or collapse the wall.

**Damp proofing.** A **DPC at plinth level** across the full wall thickness interrupts **rising damp**, which is **capillary action** through the fine pores of masonry and mortar. Because the water rises through the **material**, the remedy must be a **continuous impervious plane**, and continuity is everything — one gap defeats the whole barrier.

**Cavity walls** provide damp resistance and thermal insulation, but only if built correctly: ties **sloping down toward the outer leaf** so water runs out, **weep holes** at the base, a **DPC** stepped over openings, and the cavity kept **clear of mortar droppings**. A **mortar bridge** across the cavity conducts water straight through, and the wall then performs **worse** than a solid one because the defect is hidden.

**Reinforced masonry** places steel in the bed joints or in vertical cores of hollow blocks, greatly improving tensile and shear capacity. It is standard in seismic regions and is the basis of **confined masonry**, discussed below.

sections.heading: Earthquake resistance of masonry — the Nepali context
sections.body:
This is the most consequential material in the subchapter for Nepal, because **most of the country's building stock is load-bearing masonry** and masonry is what fails in Himalayan earthquakes.

**Why unreinforced masonry performs badly.** An earthquake applies **in-plane shear** and **out-of-plane bending** to walls that have almost no **tensile or shear strength** and almost no **ductility**. Individual wall panels then behave as **independent elements** rather than as a connected box: a wall loaded out of plane simply topples outward, taking the floor and roof it supported with it.

**The remedy is conceptual before it is technical: make the building act as a BOX.** Every measure below serves that single aim.

**NBC 202 — Mandatory Rules of Thumb for load-bearing masonry** (Nepal), together with **IS 4326**, require:

| Measure | Function |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal RC bands** at **plinth, sill, lintel and roof/floor** level, continuous around the building | **Tie the walls together** at each level so they act as one box and cannot separate at the corners |
| **Vertical reinforcement at corners, wall junctions and openings** | Resists the tension that develops from overturning and out-of-plane bending |
| **Limits on wall length between cross walls** | An unsupported long wall buckles out of plane |
| **Limits on the size and position of openings**, with piers between them | Openings interrupt the load path and concentrate stress |
| **Limits on building height and number of storeys** | Masonry's capacity is finite |
| **A rigid floor and roof diaphragm**, well connected to the walls | **Distributes the seismic force to all the walls** rather than leaving each to fend for itself |
| **Good quality mortar and units**, proper bonding | Basic material adequacy |

**The lintel band is the single most important** of the bands, because it is at the level of maximum out-of-plane response and ties the walls just below the roof. But the **roof band and the diaphragm connection** are what prevent the roof sliding off — a common and lethal failure.

**Confined masonry** is the form now recommended for new low-rise construction in Nepal: masonry walls are built **first**, then **RC tie-columns and tie-beams are cast against them**, so the concrete bonds to the toothed masonry edge. The distinction from an infill frame is important and often examined:

| | **Confined masonry** | **RC frame with masonry infill** |
|---|---|---|
| Built | **Masonry first**, then concrete cast against it | **Frame first**, then infill built into it |
| Wall's role | **Structural** — carries gravity and lateral load | Nominally non-structural, though it does resist load |
| Bond at interface | **Good** — concrete cast against toothed masonry | Poor — a construction joint |
| Behaviour | Wall and confining elements act **together** | Infill can separate, and may cause **short-column** or **soft-storey** failure |
| Suits | **Low-rise**, up to 2–3 storeys | Mid- and high-rise |

**Confined masonry's advantage** is that the confining elements prevent the wall disintegrating once it cracks — the masonry is held in place and continues to carry load, which is precisely the ductility that unreinforced masonry lacks.

**Failures observed in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake**, which are examinable as lessons:

| Failure | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Out-of-plane collapse of gable walls** | Tall, unsupported, no band at the top |
| **Corner separation** | No horizontal bands or vertical corner bars |
| **Diagonal (X) shear cracking** in piers | In-plane shear with no reinforcement |
| **Roof sliding off** | No connection between roof and walls |
| **Soft ground storey** collapse in RC frames | Open ground floor with infill above |
| **Short column** failure | Partial-height infill stiffening part of a column |
| Pounding between adjacent buildings | Inadequate separation |

**Retrofitting** existing masonry uses the same principles applied after the fact: **splint and bandage** (vertical splints at corners and horizontal bandages at band levels, in reinforced cement mortar or wire mesh), **jacketing** with ferrocement or shotcrete, **grouting** of cracks, **through-stones or stitching** across the wall thickness, **adding cross walls or buttresses**, and **strengthening the roof-to-wall connection**. The Department of Urban Development and Building Construction publishes standard retrofitting details for Nepali building types.

**Stone masonry in mud mortar** deserves a final word, because it is the commonest rural construction in Nepal's hills and the most vulnerable. Its specific weaknesses are **round or irregular stones with no through-stones**, so the wall is effectively two independent leaves of facing stone with rubble between; **weak mud mortar**; and **great wall thickness with high mass**, which increases the seismic force. The standard improvements are **through-stones at regular intervals** (tying the two faces together), **corner stones**, **horizontal bands** even of timber, and **limiting the wall height** — all achievable with local materials and unskilled labour, which is what makes them practical.

formulas.label: Effective thickness of a cavity wall (IS 1905)
formulas.expression: t_eff = GREATER of ⅔(t₁ + t₂) and the thickness of the thicker leaf
formulas.note: The ⅔ factor recognises that the leaves are tied but not bonded, so they do not act fully together.

formulas.label: Slenderness ratio of masonry
formulas.expression: λ = effective height (or length) / effective thickness ≤ 27 for load-bearing walls in cement mortar
formulas.note: Lower limits apply for weaker mortars. A half-brick wall cannot satisfy it over a storey height.

formulas.label: Permissible compressive stress in masonry
formulas.expression: permissible = basic stress × stress reduction factor × area factor × shape factor
formulas.note: Basic stress from unit strength and mortar grade; reduction factors for slenderness and eccentricity.

formulas.label: Mortar strength rule
formulas.expression: Mortar must be WEAKER than the masonry unit
formulas.note: So cracking stays fine and confined to the joints, rather than passing through the units.

formulas.label: Modular brick wall thicknesses
formulas.expression: half brick 90 mm (100 nominal) ; one brick 190 mm (200 nominal) ; traditional brick gives 115 and 230 mm
formulas.note: Modular unit 190 × 90 × 90 mm plus a 10 mm joint gives a 200 mm module.

formulas.label: Seismic bands (NBC 202 / IS 4326)
formulas.expression: Continuous horizontal RC bands at PLINTH, SILL, LINTEL and ROOF level, with vertical bars at corners and openings
formulas.note: Their purpose is to make the walls act as one BOX rather than as independent panels.

formulas.label: Response reduction factor for unreinforced masonry
formulas.expression: R = 1.5 (against 5.0 for a ductile RC frame)
formulas.note: Reflects masonry's near-absence of ductility — so it is designed for a much higher force.

formulas.label: Fibreboard density classes (IS 3348)
formulas.note: Some circulating collections misquote the medium band; the standard range is 350–800 kg/m³.
